qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE) Subject:

Under pressure and following a strike against his arrival at France Inter, journalist Charles Sapin eventually decided not to join this public media outlet. The act of censoring a journalist like this, whether for his actual or perceived political views, further tarnishes the image of the public audiovisual sector, which is increasingly and openly being monopolised by the left. Among the trade unions behind this act of censorship is the National Union of Journalists (SNJ)1. And yet, the Commission is consulting this extremist trade union, skilfully presented as a member of ‘civil society’, on topics such as freedom of the press2. 1.
Does the Commission publish a precise account of the requests and contributions made by this trade union or the European network to which it belongs3?
Does it intend to maintain relations with this far-left organisation, which is openly opposed to media pluralism and freedom of expression?

at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.11.2026) The Commission monitors the situation of media freedom and media pluralism in all Member States, including France, in its annual Rule of Law Report1. According to its methodology, the Report draws on a wide range of sources, including national authorities, independent bodies, civil society organisations, professional associations and European networks, as well as its own data gathering2. Every year, national authorities and stakeholders are invited to provide written input through a public consultation and participate in country visits held in each Member State. In 2026, the Commission held over 600 meetings with national authorities, independent bodies and stakeholders. The organisations consulted are listed in the annexes to the respective country chapters. Written contributions are published on the Commission's website with the stakeholders' agreement3. Among the key principles leading these consultations are objectivity, equal treatment and proportionality. The assessments and the recommendations are based on a careful analysis of the situation in each Member State. The Commission carries out its assessment autonomously and retains full responsibility for its findings and recommendations.
